title: After AI Takes the Talent, Only Six Tokens Are Left in Crypto
dek: Delphi's Yan Liberman says crypto VCs make one deal a year because AI has absorbed all the smart people; the only things that can still make money are a handful of tokens with real revenue that don't depend on the crypto market.
why: A frontline crypto VC publicly lays out his six positions and his reasoning, including why he no longer does crypto venture and why he has given up on gaming. High information density, but you need some crypto background.
who: Crypto fund managers, token investors, and practitioners who want to understand how a frontline crypto VC allocates capital and evaluates founders.
skip: The ad segment from 16:17 to 17:57 can be skipped.

points.h: This rally has no obvious buyer
points.body: Yan says the market was caught off guard by ‘QE in the form of long-end bond curve control’, which triggered a short squeeze, but he personally finds it hard to see new highs in the short term, because that requires a lot of new money, and the obvious buyer historically (Sailor) isn't buying now — instead he's cashmaxing and paying down preferred stock. He thinks leverage hasn't accumulated excessively, and this sequence of slow grind, pause, alt rotation is actually healthy. Another structural change is that the alt market has become shallower, money concentrates more easily into a few assets, so you don't need a whole new cohort of buyers to move the market — it has become a ‘stock-picking market’.

points.h: Buy the ones that look like hot coins but aren't as crowded
points.body: Yan admits there are only about 10 to 15 investable liquid tokens right now, and every crypto fund is already allocated to those 15. His conclusion: you should look for names that ‘look and smell like these coins, but aren't as crowded to trade’. Hyperliquid is a long-term bull, but going to 200 within four months would be surprising; for short-term excess returns you have to look at less obvious names. Santi adds that with 15 investable coins, any liquid fund going on a show repeats the same five names.

points.h: Crypto venture does one deal a year
points.body: Yan says only one of their latest venture fund's five investments is crypto, and over the past year they did only one crypto venture deal. The reason is that crypto venture's value capture and defensibility are now clearer, so you can quickly screen out a large number of projects, but the thesis that ‘crypto gets broadly adopted across multiple verticals’ has been pushed to the sidelines, and AI is a major factor in attracting talent, attention and capital. His one crypto investment is Tori Finance, a tokenized Turkish lira carry trade, dollar-hedged, about 10.5% organic yield, no incentives.

points.h: The six tokens share one thing: revenue not from crypto
points.body: Yan's six public tokens are Hyperliquid, Zcash, Lighter, Venice, Grass, Aerodrome. He says he prefers projects with a ‘revenue story’ that don't depend heavily on crypto activity, because that makes them more defensive and gives a stronger TAM story. He details Grass: projected $70 million revenue, $40 million operating profit, doing residential IP network data scraping, customers are frontier labs, token market cap $330 million, unlocks finish in October, about 30% of supply with the foundation, no equity only the foundation, and if valued as a pure-equity non-crypto business, the private market could probably raise $1 to 2 billion.

points.h: Crypto's return requirements have already changed
points.body: Yan says he no longer anchors on annualized return rates, but instead sets individual price targets, stop losses and invalidation conditions, and keeps a reserve of money for a ‘total collapse’ scenario. He admits he just likes volatility. Santi says he now doesn't do crypto venture that can't at least 10x, that Ethereum at $300 billion has no clean 10x, and that the downside asymmetry is far greater than the upside. Yan responds that comfort comes from holding ‘productive assets’ rather than ‘reflexive assets’, and the key to a productive asset is the durability of its earnings and how much it depends on reflexive assets.

points.h: The gaming vertical has been abandoned
points.body: Yan says gaming as a whole is a hard vertical to invest in, because games as a business have too short a lifecycle, and once you run the NPV the long-term value story is hard to sustain. They tried Gunzilla, a big bet, and the result was bad, which he attributes to management and spending issues rather than game quality — the game itself is AAA level, on par with Call of Duty, PUBG, Fortnite. He says this may be their last attempt at AAA level, and after that gaming as a broad category will be hard, with only small versions of games doing well. They now think the only truly investable vertical left is basically ‘financialized applications’.

points.h: Aerodrome is a classic catch-up trade
points.body: Yan says Aerodrome originally planned to migrate to mainnet in mid-July and support multichain, but it was delayed, and the price suffered as a result; the release is now set for the second half of September, migration to ETH and ARC has been announced, and whether it migrates to Robin Hood is unconfirmed. He sees this as a huge opportunity for TVL, volume and fees, and many people treat it as a catch-up trade. The prior problem was the relationship between emissions and revenue — emissions go to LPs, revenue goes to stakers, criticized as offsetting revenue with emissions. Now they want to make emissions dynamic, tied one-to-one to trading volume, so price up means emissions down; at the same time they are adding multiple revenue lines, estimated to contribute an extra 40% of revenue with no emissions offset. Currently OI relative to market cap is not a large position.

points.h: The investment committee now weighs founders most
points.body: Yan says if he could pick only one change, it's the weight of founder due diligence. In early crypto it was obvious what needed to exist, so you invested more on the idea and defensibility, with lower founder weight. But once you move into other professional verticals, you can't really diligence the idea and moat, and the only repeatable, scalable thing is the founder side. They now ask ‘what is your earliest memory, then walk us through your life’. He also mentions the ‘chip on the shoulder’ from childhood trauma and the desperate desire to win as actually valuable factors, and gives Athena's Guy as an example, saying he will stop at nothing to win.
